'''''Gaultheria procumbens''''', also called the '''eastern teaberry''', the '''checkerberry''',{{efn|This name also sometimes refers to ''[[Mitchella repens]]'' (the partridge berry).}} the '''boxberry''', or the '''American wintergreen''', is a perennial species of ''[[Gaultheria]]'' native to northeastern [[North America]] from [[Newfoundland (island)|Newfoundland]] west to southeastern [[Manitoba]], and south to [[Alabama]].<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | access-date = 2017-12-16}}</ref> It is a member of the [[Ericaceae]] (heath family).<ref name=Dwelley>{{cite book |last=Dwelley |first=Marilyn J. |year=1977 |title=Summer & Fall Wildflowers of New England |publisher=Down East Enterprise, Inc. |page=60 |isbn=978-0-89272-020-0 |url={{Google Books |id=S7gBAAAACAAJ |page=60 |plainurl=1}} |access-date=2008-08-10}}</ref>

== Growth and habitat ==
[[File:Gaultheria procumbens 6049.JPG|thumb|Flowers blooming in July in Vermont]]
''G. procumbens'' is a small, low-growing [[shrub]], typically reaching {{cvt|10|–|15|cm|in|0}} tall. The [[leaves]] are [[evergreen]], elliptic to ovate, {{cvt|2|–|5|cm|frac=4}} long and {{cvt|1|–|2|cm|frac=4}} broad, with a distinct [[oil of wintergreen]] scent.

The [[flower]]s are [[pendulous]], with a white, sometimes pink-tinged,<ref>{{Minnesota Wildflowers|flower/wintergreen|Gaultheria procumbens (Wintergreen)}}</ref> bell-shaped [[corolla (botany)|corolla]] with five teeth at the tip {{cvt|8-10|mm|2}}<!-- length of petals --> long, and above it a white [[calyx (botany)|calyx]]. They are borne in [[leaf axil]]s, usually one to three per stem. The [[anther]]s are forked somewhat like a snake's tongue, with two [[awn (botany)|awns]] at the tip.<ref name="FNA">{{eFloras|1 |first=Debra K. |last=Trock |volume=8}}</ref>

The [[fruit]] is red and {{cvt|6-9|mm|in|2}} across.<ref name="FNA" /> It is an [[epigynous berry]], with the majority of the flesh of the fruit being composed of the fleshy calyx.

The plant is a [[calcifuge]], favoring acidic soil, in pine or hardwood forests, although it generally produces fruit only in sunnier areas.<ref name="feis">{{FEIS |last=Coladonato |first=Milo |date=1994 |genus=Gaultheria |species=procumbens |type=shrub}}</ref> It often grows as part of the heath complex in an [[oak–heath forest]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dcr.virginia.gov/natural_heritage/ncTIIIe.shtml |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090115181617/http://www.dcr.virginia.gov/natural_heritage/ncTIIIe.shtml |url-status=dead |archive-date=2009-01-15 |title=Oak / Heath Forests |work=The Natural Communities of Virginia: Classification of Ecological Community Groups (Version 2.3) |publisher=Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation |date=2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dcr.virginia.gov/natural-heritage/natural-communities/nctc6 |title=Oak / Heath Forests |work=The Natural Communities of Virginia: Classification of Ecological Groups and Community Types (Version 3.0) |last1=Fleming |first1=G. P. |first2=K. D. |last2=Patterson |first3=K. |last3=Taverna |date=2017 |publisher=Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation, Division of Natural Heritage |location=Richmond |access-date=2018-08-01}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Schafale |first1=M. P. |first2=A. S. |last2=Weakley |date=1990 |title=Classification of the natural communities of North Carolina: third approximation |publisher=North Carolina Natural Heritage Program, North Carolina Division of Parks and Recreation |url=https://www.ncnhp.org/references/publications/classification-natural-communities-north-carolina-3rd-approximation}}<!-- pdf: https://files.nc.gov/dncr-nhp/documents/files/Natural-Community-Classification-Third-Approximation-1990.pdf --></ref>

''G. procumbens'' spreads by means of long [[rhizome]]s, which are within the top {{cvt|2|–|3|cm|in|frac=4}} of soil. Because of the shallow nature of the rhizomes, it does not survive most forest fires, but a brief or mild fire may leave rhizomes intact, from which the plant can regrow even if the above-ground shrub was consumed.<ref name="feis"/>

This plant has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name=AGM>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/details?plantid=842 |title=Gaultheria procumbens |work=RHS Gardening |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |date=2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 39 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 28 July 2018}}</ref>

==Edibility==
The fruits of ''G. procumbens,'' considered its actual "teaberries", are edible, with a taste of mildly sweet [[wintergreen]] similar to the flavors of the ''[[Mentha]]'' varieties ''[[Mentha piperita|M. piperita]]'' (peppermint) and ''[[Mentha spicata|M. spicata]]'' (spearmint) even though ''G. procumbens'' is not a true mint. The leaves and branches make a fine [[herbal tea]] through the normal drying and infusion process. For the leaves to yield significant amounts of their essential oil, they need to be fermented for at least three days.<ref name=HealthfulHerb>{{cite book |last=Gibbons |first=Euell |title=Stalking the Healthful Herbs |place=New York |publisher=David McKay |date=1966 |page=92}}</ref> The berries and leaves contain [[methyl salicylate]], a compound that is closely related to [[aspirin]].<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|pages=150|oclc=244766414|orig-year=1982}}</ref>

Teaberry extract can be used to flavor tea, candy, medicine, and [[chewing gum]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering| last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-year=1979|publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=499}}</ref> Teaberry is also a regional [[Teaberry ice cream|flavor]] of [[ice cream]] in [[Pennsylvania]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Maslovara |first=Vedran |date=2022-03-23 |title=The Ice Cream Flavor You Can (Almost) Only Find In Pennsylvania |url=https://www.mashed.com/807715/the-ice-cream-flavor-you-can-almost-only-find-in-pennsylvania/ |access-date=2023-11-26 |website=Mashed |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Grossinger |first=Zoe |date=2019-07-10 |title=Why this bright pink ice cream is the most-searched flavor in PA |url=http://billypenn.com/2019/07/10/why-is-teaberry-ice-cream-the-most-searched-flavor-in-pennsylvania/ |access-date=2023-11-26 |website=Billy Penn at WHYY |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Bombay |first=Brandon |date=2023-07-07 |title=The Beloved Pennsylvania Ice Cream That Some Say Tastes Like Medicine |url=https://www.thedailymeal.com/1333612/popular-pennsylvania-ice-cream-teaberry-taste/ |access-date=2023-11-26 |website=The Daily Meal |language=en-US}}</ref> It likewise inspired the name of [[Clark's Teaberry]] chewing gum.

== Wildlife value ==
Wintergreen is not consumed in large quantities by any species of wildlife, but its regular use enhances its importance. Its fruit persists through the winter, and it is one of the few sources of green leaves available during this time. [[White-tailed deer]] browse wintergreen throughout its range, and in some localities, it is an important winter food. Other animals that eat wintergreen are [[wild turkey]], [[sharp-tailed grouse]], [[northern bobwhite]], [[ring-necked pheasant]], [[American Black Bear|black bear]], [[white-footed mouse]], and [[red fox]].  Wintergreen is a favorite food of the [[eastern chipmunk]], and the leaves are a minor winter food of the [[Eastern Gray Squirrel|gray squirrel]] in Virginia.<ref name="feis" />

== Common names ==
Other common names for ''G. procumbens'' include American mountain tea, boxberry, Canada tea, canterberry, checkerberry, chickenberry, creeping wintergreen, deerberry, drunkards, gingerberry, greenberry, ground berry, ground tea, grouseberry, hillberry, mountain tea, one-berry, proclaim, red pollom, spice berry, squaw vine, star berry, spiceberry, spicy wintergreen, spring wintergreen, teaberry, wax cluster, and youngsters.<ref name=AGM /><ref name=Lust>{{cite book|last=Lust|first=John|year=1974|title=The Herb Book|publisher=Bantam Books|page=404|isbn=978-0-553-26770-9|url={{Google Books |id=FjkMAAAACAAJ |page=404 |plainurl=1}} |access-date=2008-08-10}}</ref>

While this plant is sometimes mistakenly known as partridge berry,<ref name=Hall>{{cite book|last=Hall|first=Joan Houston|year=2002|title=Dictionary of American Regional English|publisher=Harvard University Press|page=47|isbn=978-0-674-00884-7|url={{Google Books |id=i33BWgxbvXgC |page=47 |plainurl=1}} |access-date=2007-11-16}}</ref> that name more often refers to the ground cover ''[[Mitchella repens]].''

==Traditional use==
Various Native American tribes have used the plant for medicinal purposes. The Delaware, Mohicans, and several other tribes made a tea from wintergreen leaves to treat kidney disorders. The Great Lakes and Eastern Woodlands tribes used a wintergreen poultice as a topical treatment for arthritic pain.<ref>{{cite web|url={{Google Books|id=h3Xcj5lw4rIC |page=79|plainurl=1}} |title=Secrets of Native American Herbal Remedies |first=Anthony J. |last=Cichoke |date=2001 |publisher=[[Avery Publishing|Avery]]}}</ref>
